summary: Describes MIKEY, a key management scheme for real-time multimedia, covering both two-party and group communication. Its main use is providing keys to the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP), so encrypted calls and streams can start with shared secrets set up efficiently.

plainLanguage.summary: MIKEY helps real-time media participants agree on keys and settings for protecting their streams. It offers three ways to establish shared key material and derives separate traffic keys from it.

subtitle: A key-management protocol for setting up protected real-time media sessions.

tldr.problem: Real-time media protocols need keys and security settings before protected traffic can flow. MIKEY aims to provide this setup with low bandwidth, low computation and few message exchanges.
tldr.mechanism: The parties agree or establish a TEK Generation Key using a pre-shared key, public-key encryption or Diffie-Hellman. MIKEY derives traffic keys from that shared key and sends the parameters to the security protocol.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3830 describes MIKEY, especially its use with SRTP. It is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 4738 and RFC 6309.

facts.label: RAND for key derivation
facts.value: At least 128 bits; encoded length SHOULD be at least 16 bytes

today: RFC 3830 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 4738 and RFC 6309. The RFC describes MIKEY as a key-management scheme, particularly for SRTP.

sections.title: The Key Setup Problem
sections.content:
A security protocol for real-time media needs keys and related parameters before it can protect a stream. MIKEY is a key-management scheme designed for multimedia sessions such as those using the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP).

The RFC focuses on peer-to-peer communication, simple one-to-many streams and small interactive groups. Its design goals include end-to-end security, efficient messages and the ability to carry MIKEY within session setup protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Media encryption needs the participants to agree on keys first. MIKEY sets up those keys and settings for real-time streams.

sections.title: From a Shared Key to Media Keys
sections.content:
A TEK Generation Key (TGK) is shared key material from which MIKEY derives one or more Traffic-Encrypting Keys (TEKs). A TEK and the security protocol's parameters form a Data Security Association, which the security protocol uses to protect traffic.

A Crypto Session is a stream, or set of related streams, protected by one security-protocol instance. A Crypto Session Bundle groups one or more Crypto Sessions. Sessions in a bundle can share a TGK but receive distinct TEKs.
sections.plainLanguage: The parties first establish a shared key called a TGK. MIKEY derives a separate traffic key for each Crypto Session from it.

sections.title: Three Key Establishment Methods
sections.content:
Each method uses a timestamp to help detect replay and a random value called RAND for key derivation. In the pre-shared-key method, the Initiator sends the TGK encrypted with keys derived from the shared secret and includes a message authentication code. A verification reply is optional. This method is mandatory to implement.

In the public-key method, the Initiator encrypts an envelope key to the Responder's public key, then uses that envelope key to protect the TGK. The message is signed, and this method is mandatory to implement. In the Diffie-Hellman method, the parties exchange signed public values and independently derive a TGK; it is optional to implement, requires certificates and provides perfect forward secrecy.
sections.plainLanguage: MIKEY can use a secret the parties already share, encrypt a new key to the receiver, or derive a key through Diffie-Hellman. Each method has different requirements and security properties.

sections.title: Deriving Keys and Choosing Algorithms
sections.content:
MIKEY uses a pseudo-random function based on HMAC with SHA-1 to derive keys. The inputs include the master key, session identifiers and RAND. The random value used for key derivation must be at least 128 bits; its encoded length should be at least 16 bytes.

The RFC requires implementations to support SHA-1, AES counter mode with a 128-bit key for key transport, and HMAC-SHA-1 with a 160-bit tag. It also defines defaults for public-key encryption and signatures. A security policy payload carries settings for the data security protocol, including SRTP parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: MIKEY uses a defined calculation to turn shared key material into the keys a media protocol needs. The RFC sets a required baseline of algorithms and lets messages carry protocol settings.

sections.title: Messages, Updates and Replay Checks
sections.content:
A MIKEY message starts with a common header followed by payloads. Each payload identifies the next one, and a MAC or signature comes last. The header includes the MIKEY version, message type, Crypto Session Bundle ID and information for mapping Crypto Sessions to security-protocol sessions.

To update a bundle, the parties run MIKEY again using the same bundle ID and a new timestamp. The update must not include a new RAND. Receivers check timestamps and a cache of authenticated messages to reject outdated or replayed messages. This avoids a challenge-response exchange but requires loosely synchronized clocks.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIKEY message is an ordered set of labeled payloads. Timestamps and a cache of accepted messages help the receiver reject copied or outdated requests.

sections.title: Transport and Group Use
sections.content:
MIKEY can be carried within session setup protocols, including the SIP/SDP and RTSP integrations identified by the RFC. MIKEY itself does not carry network addresses or ports. For SRTP, the stream identifier helps retrieve the correct Data Security Association.

For a simple one-to-many stream, a server can send the same TGK to multiple receivers using the pre-shared-key or public-key method. Small interactive groups can use separate unicast SRTP streams. The Diffie-Hellman method creates a distinct key for each pair and cannot establish a group key.
sections.plainLanguage: MIKEY can be included in a session setup exchange. A server can distribute shared key material to a small streaming group, while interactive groups can set up separate outgoing streams.

sections.title: Key Exposure and Other Risks
sections.content:
The key-establishment method must provide protection at least as strong as the media encryption requires. The Initiator generates the TGK in the pre-shared-key and public-key methods, so a poor random-number generator can weaken those methods. Neither method provides perfect forward secrecy; the Diffie-Hellman method does, when authenticated with signatures to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks.

If a TGK is exposed, all TEKs derived from it are compromised. Exposure of one TEK does not by itself expose other TEKs derived from the TGK. The RFC also discusses replay-cache limits, denial-of-service risks and the fact that identity protection is not a main design goal.
sections.plainLanguage: The security of the key exchange must match the protection needed for the media. A leaked TGK exposes its derived traffic keys, while Diffie-Hellman is the only method here that provides perfect forward secrecy.
